5.14.m: Śeṣa said: / Then the bull among men, the king, wishing to hear / The excellent tale of the lord of the Raghus, spoke to Śatrughna, who was pleased with his welcome.
Sumada said: / “Is Rāma, the crest-jewel of all the worlds, living happily? / He is the incarnation for the protection of devotees, the bestower of grace upon me.
Blessed are those people in the city who continually drink in / The lotus-face of the lord of the Raghus with the cups of their eyes, greatly delighted.
All my collection of wealth, O bull among men, / And all the collection of objects such as my ancestral land, have become truly fulfilled, O wise one.
A favor was previously granted to me by Kāmākṣā, melted with compassion: / ‘Together with your family, you will behold the lotus-face of the lord of the Raghus.’”
When that hero Sumada, the best of rulers, had spoken thus, / he related all that arising of the virtues of the lord of the Raghus.
After staying there for three nights, the wise younger brother of the lord of the Raghus / Formed the intention to depart along with the king.
Learning that, Sumada quickly anointed his son in the kingship, / Approved by the great king Śatrughna and by Puṣkala.
The wise king then gave clothes, numerous gems, / And diverse wealth to the servants of Śatrughna.
Then he began his march with ministers who were great knowers of wealth, / With infantry, cavalry, elephants, excellent steeds, and crores of chariots.
Accompanied by that bowman Sumada, / Śatrughna, bearing the majesty of the lord of the Raghus, proceeded along the road smiling.
Reaching the bank of the Payoṣṇī river, that noble horse advanced; / All the warriors guarding the horse followed behind it.
Seeing various hermitages of ṛṣis who performed great austerities, / Hearing everywhere the arising of the virtues of the lord of the Raghus:
“Here goes the wise Hari, protected by Hari, / Constantly by Haris, by devotees of Hari, and by followers of the foremost of Haris.”
Hearing these auspicious words of the sages all around, / the great lord was pleased with those whose mental states were filled with devotion.
And he saw a pure hermitage filled with people and creatures, / Where all inauspiciousness was destroyed for men who heard the chanting of the Vedas,
The entire sky purified by the smoke of sacrificial offerings of the agnihotra, / Looking splendid with many sacrificial posts erected by foremost sages,
Where cows fit to be protected are cared for by deer, / And mice dig no holes in this place out of fear of cats;
Serpents play constantly with peacocks and mongooses; / Elephants and lions dwell here continually, having attained friendship;
Gazelles taking delight in grazing on the wild rice growing there / Have no fear of death, protected by the hosts of sages;
Cows whose udders are like water jars and whose forms resemble Nandinī / Purify the earth with the dust raised by their hooves.
Seeing the foremost sages engaged in righteous deeds with lotus hands bearing sacrificial wood, / He asked the all-knowing Sumati, the minister of Rāma.
Śatrughna said: / “O Sumati, whose hermitage is this that shines ahead, / To be frequented by non-hostile creatures, filled with hosts of sages?
I wish to hear the account of the sage, and I shall purify / My own body through stories and descriptions of him.”
Hearing that momentous speech of the great-souled Śatrughna, / the minister related [the story] of the wise lord of the Raghus.
Sumati said: / "Know this to be the hermitage of Cyavana, adorned with great ascetics, / filled with creatures free from enmity, and crowded with the wives of sages.
He is that great sage who assigned a sacrificial share to the two physicians of heaven / at the great sacrifice of Svāyambhuva, breaking the pride of Indra.
This power of the great sage, rich in the strength of austerities / and embodying the Vedas, cannot be encompassed by anyone."
Hearing the account of the great sage Cyavana, the younger brother of Rāma / asked Sumati all about the crushing of Indra's pride and the rest.
Śatrughna said: / "When did he assign a share to the two Aśvins among the rows of gods? / What was done by the king of the gods at the great sacrifice of Svāyambhuva?"
Sumati said: / In the lineage of Brahmā was a sage widely renowned by the name of Bhṛgu. / Once he went at evening to fetch sacrificial firewood.
Then, to destroy the sacrifice, the mighty rākṣasa Damana / came and loudly uttered these terrifying words:
"Where is that relative of sages, and where is his faultless woman?" / Overwhelmed with wrath, he spoke these words again and again.
Then the sacrificial fire, knowing the danger that had come from the rākṣasa, / showed him his irreproachable, pregnant wife.
The rākṣasa seized her as she wept like an osprey: / "O Bhṛgu, protect me! O husband, protect me! Protect me, O lord, O treasure of austerities!"
Taking her as she was thus crying out in distress, he went outside, / that wicked one threatening the chaste wife of Bhṛgu with a shower of words.
Then, terrified with great fear, from the midst of the womb / the fetus fell out, with blazing eyes, his offspring like the fire itself.
By him it was said: "Do not go! Quickly turn to ashes, O extremely evil-minded one! / Truly, having laid hands on a virtuous woman, you will not attain welfare!"
Addressed thus, he fell swiftly, his body turned to ashes; / then the mother, taking the child, went to the hermitage, agitated in mind.
Bhṛgu, having learned all that was done by the fire, overwhelmed with wrath, / cursed him: "Become an eater of everything, O informer to a wicked enemy!"
Then, being cursed, deeply afflicted by grief, the Fire grasped his feet: / "Grant me grace, O master, O ocean of compassion, O great-minded one!
A true word was spoken by me out of fear, not out of malice toward the spiritual teacher; / therefore, show mercy upon me, O crest-jewel of righteousness!"
Then he granted grace: "And though an eater of everything, you shall be pure." / Thus said the ascetic sage, melted with pity, to the eater of oblations.
For the son who had fallen from the womb, the pure Brahmin, / holding darbha grass in his hand and highly auspicious, performed the birth rites and the like according to rule.
Because of his falling [from the womb], all the ascetics called the son Cyavana. / Slowly he grew, like the moon on the first day of the bright fortnight.
He went to perform austerities to the Revā, the sole purifier of the worlds, / surrounded by all his disciples endowed with the power of austerities.
Having gone there, the great one performed austerities for ten thousand years; / on his shoulders grew two kiṃśuka trees, adorned atop an anthill.
Deer came and eagerly scratched themselves against his body; / enveloped in irresistible austerities, he knew nothing at all.
Once, Manu the lord, setting out on a pilgrimage to sacred places, / went to the Revā with his family, surrounded by a great army.
Having bathed there in the great river and gratified the ancestors and gods, / he gave gifts to the brāhmaṇas for the propitiation of Viṣṇu.
Wandering here and there within the forest, that daughter of his, / charming and adorned with burnished gold, was accompanied by her female companions.
Then, seeing an anthill there adorned by a great tree, / she beheld a certain radiant energy without winking or blinking.
Going there, she pierced it with splinters, and blood flowed forth. / Seeing it, the king's daughter fell into distress, extremely sorrowful.
Overwhelmed by her offense, she told neither her mother nor her father; / stricken with fear, she grieved within herself all alone.
Then the earth trembled, O king, and meteors fell from the sky; / all the directions turned smoky, and the sun was encircled by a halo.
Then the king's horses were lost, and many elephants died; / wealth consisting of jewels was destroyed, and mutual quarrel arose then.
Seeing that, the king, frightened and somewhat perturbed in mind, / asked the people: “Has anyone committed an offense against a sage?”
Learning through report of that deed done by his daughter, / he went there, deeply sorrowful, together with his full army and mounts.
Beholding that receptacle of austerity endowed with great ascetic power, / he praised him and appeased him: “O best of sages, show compassion!”
Pleased with him, that best of sages, rich in austerities, said: / “All this portending evil has been done by your daughter; understand that.
O great king, your daughter has pierced out my eyes; / much blood flowed out, yet knowing this, she did not speak to you.
Therefore, O great king, she must be given to me according to rule; / then the pacification of the portents will follow, without doubt.”
Hearing that, the sorrowful king, whose understanding was his eye, gave his daughter, / endowed with noble family, youth, beauty, good conduct, and auspicious marks.
When this lotus-eyed maiden was given by the king, / then all the portents arising from the sage's anger came to an end.
Having given his daughter to that sage, the receptacle of austerities, / the king returned to his own city, sorrowful and filled with pity.

5.15.m:
Sumati said: / Then the sage, having gone to his own hermitage together with his wife, the daughter of Manu, / who was endowed with yoga, attained joy, his sins entirely destroyed.

She [served] her husband, an excellent mortal, / deprived of sight, his vitality gone through old age,

she served him, the foremost of pure intellect, / just as one serves one's family deity who bestows desired desires.

Serving her husband, discerning his intentions, / the noble one, a treasury of austerities, her beloved,
the lovely and chaste woman attained supreme joy, / just as Śacī intent on serving Indra.
The slender princess, endowed with all auspicious marks / and lovely-limbed, served his feet, subsisting on fruit, roots, and water.
Always devoted to carrying out his word, intent on worshiping him, / delighting in the welfare of all beings, she spent her time.
Casting away lust, hypocrisy, malice, greed, sin, and arrogance, / ever vigilant and eager, she fully pleased Cyavana.
Performing service to him in this manner with speech, body, and deeds / for a thousand years, O great king, she held desires in her heart.
Once, the two physicians of the gods arrived at the sage's hermitage. / Having properly welcomed them with hospitality, she honored them.

Their hearts pleased by the worship, water for argha and pādya, and the like offered by Śaryāti's daughter, / the two handsome ones, moved by affection, said to that lovely-limbed woman: / “Choose a boon!”
Seeing those two physicians of the gods pleased, / the king's daughter, best among the wise, set her mind on asking a boon.
Discerning her husband's wish, the princess spoke: / “If you two gods are pleased, let two eyes be granted to my husband!”
Hearing this charming speech of Sukanyā / and beholding this fidelity, the two best of physicians said:
“If this husband of yours allots a share in the sacrifice for the gods to us, / we shall now restore clear vision to his eyes.”
Cyavana also said, “So be it,” regarding giving a share to the two of excellent splendour. / Then the delighted Aśvins said to that best of ascetics:
“May you plunge into this pool fashioned by the Siddhas!” / Thus addressed, he whose body was seized by decrepitude and covered with prominent veins
was led into the pool by the two Aśvins, and they themselves plunged into the pool. / Then three men emerged, handsome and dear to women,
wearing golden garlands and earrings, identical in appearance, and finely clad. / Seeing them, lovely of form and resplendent like the sun, that woman of fair hips,
not recognizing her husband, the virtuous woman took refuge with the Aśvins. / Showing her husband to her, they were pleased with her devotion to her husband;
bidding farewell to the sage, they went by celestial chariot to heaven, / carrying the purpose of receiving their own share in the sacrifice to be performed.

Seeing her emaciated after a long time and weakened by the practice of vows, / [the sage], stirred with compassion, spoke with a voice trembling with love:

"Today I am pleased, O proud woman, with you who bestow honor, / by your supreme service and undivided devotion in your heart.
for your own body, which is such a dear friend to embodied beings, / you did not regard as something proper to preserve for your own sake.

The divine graces won by me, devoted to my own dharma, through austerity, meditation, knowledge, and spiritual yoga— / behold, through your service to me, I grant to you those very graces, unhindered, fearless, and free from grief.

Other [worldly pleasures] are dispelled by the mere movement of the brows of the Lord of wide strides [Viṣṇu]; / you have attained perfection: enjoy heavenly splendors, yielding the fruits of your own dharma, unattainable to mortals through royal transformations!”

As he spoke thus, the woman, seeing him expert in all the arts / of yoga and illusion, became free of anxiety.

With words faltering with modesty and affection, her face blooming with a shy glance and a smile, she said:

“O best of brāhmaṇas, lord of unfailing yogic power! O master, I know that all this is accomplished in you, my husband.

The agreement that was declared by you, that bodily union should occur once— / let there be an excellent offspring, the virtue of chaste wives.

Having taught her what was to be done there according to instruction, / by which this very body, severely emaciated, was made fit for pleasure,
may be revived for you when overcome by desire; / and indicate, O lord, a suitable dwelling for this wretched woman.”
Sumati said: / Wishing to please his beloved, Cyavana resorted to yoga, / O king, and at that very moment created a celestial chariot that went at will,
granting all desires, lovely, adorned with all manner of jewels, / yielding an increase of all purposes, embellished with jeweled pillars,
provided with divine coverings, bringing comfort in all seasons, / and decorated with variegated ribbons and banners.
resplendent with garlands, variegated wreaths, and softly buzzing six-footed [bees], / with fine silks, linens, silken garments, and varied textiles;
delightful with cushions arranged one above the other / in separate chambers, with couches, fans, and other comforts;
adorned with various crafts placed here and there, / endowed with a vast emerald pavement and coral alters;
shining with coral thresholds and diamond doors at the entrances, / crowned with golden pitchers upon sapphiric pinnacles;
furnished with diamond walls featuring foremost lustrous rubies, / endowed with multicolored canopies hung with pearl necklaces;
filled with the cooing of flocks of swans and pigeons here and there, / who repeatedly perched upon them, mistaking them for real;
with pleasure-grounds, resting areas, bedchambers, courtyards, and terraces, / built to one's pleasure, as if to astonish oneself.
To her who was thus gazing at the palace with a mind not very pleased, / he who knew the hearts of all living beings said of his own accord:
“O timid one, dive into this pool and mount this celestial chariot.” / Taking the words of her husband, the fair-browed and lotus-eyed woman,
wearing dusty clothes, her hair tied in a single braid, / her limbs covered with dirt and mud, her breasts soiled,
entered that pool of auspicious waters with joy. / Within the pool, inside a dwelling, she saw a thousand maidens,
all in the prime of youth and smelling of blue lotuses. / Seeing her, the women rose quickly and, with folded hands, said:
“We are your maidservants; command us, what shall we do?” / Having bathed that high-minded lady with a precious bath,
they gave her spotless, brand-new silk garments, O honor-giver, / and most precious ornaments, superior and resplendent;
food endowed with all virtues, and a beverage of nectar-like liquor. / Then, [looking] in a mirror, [she saw] herself garlanded, in dust-free clothes,
blessed with propitiatory rites by them, highly honored by the maidens, / and adorned with a priceless necklace and an auspicious ornament,
with a golden torque on her neck, bracelets, tinkling golden anklets, / and a golden girdle studded with many jewels resting upon her hips;
with fair eyebrows, lovely teeth, eyes white and glossy at the corners, / and a radiant face with curling dark locks rivaling the calyx of a lotus.
When she remembered her beloved husband, dear to the sages, / she was right there with the women where that lord of sages was.
Then, seeing herself in front of her husband surrounded by a thousand women, / and noticing that power of his yoga, she fell into wonder.
Seeing her cleansed of dirt by bathing, shining as never before, / wearing her own natural beauty, her lovely breasts covered,

attended by a thousand Vidyādharīs, and well-dressed, / he felt affection, O slayer of foes, and caused her to mount the aerial chariot.

In that aerial chariot, his grandeur undiminished, united with his beloved, / his body attended upon by Vidyādharīs,
he shone, lovely, having a throng of blossoming white water-lilies, / like the moon standing in the sky, surrounded by stars.

With her, in the valleys of the lordly mountain ranges where the eight protectors of the world sport, / delightful with breezes that are friends of the god of love, / resounding with the auspicious roar of the falling heavenly river and praised by Siddhas, / he, attended by a host of women, sported for a long time like Kubera.
In Vaiśrambhaka, in the divine forest, in Nandana, in Puṣpabhadraka, / in Mānasa, and in Caitraratha, he took delight, sporting with his lovely wife.

5.16.m: Sumati said: / Thus sporting with her everywhere on the surface of the earth, / he did not notice the passing of years numbered in hundreds.
Then, realizing that time was slipping away, the brāhmaṇa, / seeing that his beloved, excellent wife was fulfilled in her desires,
returned to his excellent hermitage situated on the bank of the Payoṣṇī, / teeming with non-violent creatures and frequented by deer.
There he dwelt, of great austerity, his feet constantly served / by disciples endowed with the Vedas, and performed supreme austerities.
Then once, Śaryāti wished to sacrifice to the gods; / then he sent servants to bring Cyavana.
Summoned by them, the best of the twice-born, of great austerities, came there / with Sukanyā, his lawful wife devoted to righteous conduct.
The highly renowned king saw that best of sages arrived with his wife and daughter; / beside his daughter he saw a man radiant as the sun.

The king said to his daughter, who had made obeisance at his feet, / without uttering blessings, his mind not very pleased:

"What is this that you wish to do? By you your husband, / the sage worshipped by the world, has been deceived!"
Abandoning your husband who was seized by old age and not to your liking, / you are courting this traveler as a paramour!

How has your mind strayed from the path of the virtuous? This is a disgrace to your family from which you are born; / since you shamelessly keep a paramour and drag me, your father, and your husband down!”
Smiling with pure smiles at her father who spoke thus, / she said, “Father, this is your son-in-law, the descendant of Bhṛgu.”
She related to her father the entire attainment of youth and beauty; / astonished and exceedingly delighted, he embraced his daughter.
He made the hero sacrifice with soma, and took a draught of soma for the two Aśvins / by his own brilliance, even though they were non-drinkers of soma.
Endowed with the power of austerity, he caused [them] to take the draught. / But Indra, taking his thunderbolt, approached to slay that best of brāhmaṇas,
who was making the two gods, unfit to sit in the row [of sacrificial drinkers], eligible for the row. / Seeing Indra carrying the thunderbolt, ready to slay him, the sage,
wise, uttered the sound ‘huṃ’ and paralyzed his arm. / There Indra was seen by all men with his arm paralyzed,
hissing with rage like a snake restrained by a mantra. / With his arm paralyzed, Indra praised that sage, the treasure of austerities,
who was offering the share to the two Aśvins, fearless within. / He said, “O master, let the oblation be given to the Aśvins;
it is not prevented by me, father; forgive the great offense committed [by me].” / Addressed thus, that sage, a treasure of compassion, quickly gave up his anger.
Indra's arm was freed at that time, O bull among men. / Seeing this, all the people were filled with wonder in their minds;
they praised the power of the brāhmaṇa, which was difficult even for the gods to attain. / Then the great king gave much wealth to the brāhmaṇas,
and performed the concluding purificatory bath at the end of the sacrifice, tormenting his foes. / What was asked by you: ‘Relate the great glory of Cyavana’—
all that, joined with austerity and yoga, has been told by me. / Having paid homage to this embodiment of austerity and obtained blessings of victory,
send him together with his wife to Rāma's charming sacrifice.” / Śeṣa said: / While the two were thus conversing, the horse reached the hermitage,
making [tracks] marked by its hooves on the earth with the speed of the wind, / grazing on shoots of dūrvā grass with the tip of its mouth there in the great hermitage,
while the sages, having taken sacrificial grass, had gone to the river to bathe. / Śatrughna, the tormentor of the enemy's army, esteemed by the brave,
Just then he reached the splendid dwelling of the sage Cyavana. / Going into his hermitage, the hero saw the sage Cyavana,
sitting beside Sukanyā as if asceticism embodied. / He bowed down to his feet, declaring his own name:
“I am Śatrughna, brother of the lord of the Raghus, protector of the horse.
I bow down to you for the pacification of great sins.” / Hearing these words, the best of sages spoke:
“Śatrughna, may there be welfare for you, O best of the excellent among men! / While protecting the sacrifice, may your fame become vast!
Behold the wonder, O Brahmins: Rāma too performs a sacrifice, / he whose name-remembrance and the like destroy sins!
Men burdened with great sins, delighting in others' wives, / intent on remembering his name, attain the supreme state, liberated.
By the dust arising from his lotus foot, [she who] had the form of a rock, / Gautama's half-body [Ahalyā], instantly assumed an enchanting form.
Filled with love through meditation on my own form, / having burned the heap of all sins, she attained a beautiful form.
The Daityas who beheld his captivating form on the field of battle / obtained his form, free of imperfection.
Yogins steadfast in meditation who, established in yoga, meditate on him, / are freed from the fear of saṃsāra and go to the supreme state.
Blessed am I! Today I shall see the splendid face of Rāma, / with eye-corners like lotus petals, a fine nose, beautiful brows, and high-raised [features].
That tongue which lovingly recites the name of the lord of Raghus is [a true tongue]; / the contrary one is just like a serpent's tongue.
Today the merit of my asceticism is attained; today my desires are fulfilled, / since I shall see the face of Rāmacandra, hard to reach even for Brahmā and others.
With the dust of his feet I make my limbs pure; / with varied tales [of him] I will purify my tongue.”

With tears and faltering voice flowing from the mass of love awakened by remembering the feet of Rāma: / "O glorious Rāmacandra, best of the Raghus, embodiment of dharma, / compassionate to devotees, deliver me from worldly existence!"
babbling thus before the sages, his eyes filled with tears, / he, remaining in meditation, did not perceive anything around him as foreign or his own.
Śatrughna said to that sage: “Master, let our excellent sacrifice / be made most pure by the dust of your feet!
It is great fortune for the lord of the Raghus if that mighty-armed one, / honored by all the world, abides within your heart.”
Addressed thus, Cyavana, with his attendants and surrounded by all the sacred fires, / went there, submerged in a lake of joy.
Hanūmat, seeing that devotee of Rāma going on foot, / spoke this word full of humility to Śatrughna:
“Master, if you say so, I will carry this best of sages, / handsome as a great man and a devotee of Rāma, to his city.”
Hearing that momentous speech of the monkey-hero, the slayer of foes / commanded Hanumat: "Go, bring that sage!"
Mounting the sage with his family upon his own back, the swift Hanūmat / carried him quickly, like the wind going everywhere in the sky.
Seeing that the sage had arrived, Rāma, the best of the wise, / offered the arghya, pādya, and the rest, delighted and overwhelmed with affection.
“Blessed am I now by the sight of you, best of sages! / My sacrifice, supplied with all provisions, is sanctified.”
Hearing this speech, Cyavana, the best of sages, / his limbs thrilling with hair standing on end from love, spoke, exceedingly joyful:
“Master, for you, a god to Brahmins and one who protects the path of dharma, / the honoring of Brahmins is entirely fitting, O great king!”

5.17.m: Śeṣa said: / Then Śatrughna, seeing the inconceivable ascetic power of Cyavana, / praised the brāhmanic asceticism, praised alone by all the world:
“Ah, behold the accomplishment of yoga in this best of Brahmins, / who in an instant caused to be made that celestial chariot so difficult to obtain!
Where is that great attainment of enjoyment of pure-souled sages, / and where is the desire for enjoyment of mortal souls devoid of ascetic power?”
Wishing thus to himself, Śatrughna stayed for a moment / in Cyavana's hermitage, drank water, and attained pleasant comfort.
Having drunk the water of that holy-watered river named Payoṣṇī, / the great horse, moving with the speed of the wind, went on along the path.
Seeing its departure, the warriors then followed behind, / some on elephants, [some] on foot, some in chariots, and some on horses.
Śatrughna, accompanied by the excellent minister named Sumati, / quickly followed behind in a chariot adorned with horses.
Advancing, the horse reached the city of the king named Vimala, / named Ratnātaṭa, crowded with delighted and well-nourished people.
Hearing from a servant that the excellent horse of the lord of the Raghus / had indeed arrived near the city, accompanied by all the warriors,
then [the king], with seventy elephants of the color of the moon, / with tens of thousands of horses, with golden-lustred chariots,
and accompanied by a thousand [chariots], went toward Śatrughna. / Having bowed down to Śatrughna and to all the great car-warriors who had arrived,

and offering to him his treasury of wealth, all his goods, and his kingdom, / the king, standing before him, said, “What shall I do?”

The king also, great in majesty, firmly embraced with both arms / his [son] who was bowed at his feet.
Having placed his entire kingdom in the charge of his son, he went along, / surrounded by many archers.
Hearing the name of Rāmacandra, captivating to every ear, / everyone, bowing down to that horse, gave great wealth and goods.
Having honored the king with supreme joy, / Śatrughna then went behind the horse along with his army.
Proceeding thus on that path, he saw a foremost mountain, / shining with crystal, golden, and silver rows of plateaus,
resounding with waterfalls, its ground having various minerals, / adorned with lacquer-red color and good minerals such as red chalk,
where wives of Siddhas play with Siddhas, free from fear, / where Gandharvas, Apsarases, and Nāgas sport at ease,
served by cool winds that touch the waves of the Gaṅgā, / beautifully adorned with the sounds of lutes, resonant geese, and parrots.
Looking at the mountain, his mind overcome by the wonder born from seeing it, / Śatrughna said this to Sumati:
“What is this great, foremost mountain that fills my mind with wonder? / A wondrous [mountain] with noble plateaus of silver shines on my path.
Is this an abode of deities, a sporting ground of the gods, / since it agitates my mind with its collections of beauty?”
Hearing this speech, Sumati then spoke, / his intellect set upon the lotus feet of Rāmacandra, the abode of virtues to be proclaimed.

“O King, ruler of the earth, this Nīla mountain shines ahead,
with delightful, lofty peaks and crystal summits on all sides.

Sinners delighting in other men's wives do not see it;
the lowest of men do not acknowledge Viṣṇu's host of virtues.

Those whose thinking is based on rationalistic arguments originating in their own intellect
do not acknowledge the dharma arising from śruti and smṛti, which is well established by the virtuous.

Sellers of indigo, sellers of lac,
a brāhmaṇa who sells clarified butter and the like, a drinker of liquor,

a father who does not give his daughter endowed with beauty to one of good family and conduct,
[but] sells her out of greed for wealth, deluded by sin,

a man who wrongs his wife endowed with good family and conduct,
who eats sweets alone and does not give to his kinsmen,

who discriminates in cooking for a brāhmaṇa at a meal,
or an evil-minded person who does not have kṛsara or pāyasa given to a petitioner,

those who slight guests scorched by the heat of the sun,
those who partake of food in the sky, and those who betray trust,

those who turn their backs on Raghunātha—they do not see [it], O great king.
This holy, supreme mountain is adorned by Puruṣottama;

delightful, it purifies all through its sight.
Here stands he whose feet are worshipped by the diadems of the gods,

worthy of being seen by the virtuous, the giver of merit, Puruṣottama,
whom the Vedas do not know, declaring ‘not this, not this’,

the dust of whose feet is sought by Indra and other gods and is very hard to obtain,
whom the wise know through the flawless statements of the Vedānta and other teachings.

That glorious Puruṣottama resides here on Nīla mountain.
Ascending it, bowing to him, worshipping him with pious acts and the like,

and eating the food offering, O king, one becomes four-armed.
In this connection, they cite this ancient legendary history.

Hear it, O great king, filled with all kinds of wonders,
the story of King Ratnagrīva and his family,

how he attained the four-armed state and other [blessings] hard to obtain even for gods and demons.
There was, O great king, a city famed in the worlds as Kāñcī,

abounding in troops and mounts, with a retinue of noble men,
in which dwell foremost brāhmaṇas deeply devoted to the six duties,

intent on the welfare of all beings, eager in devotion to Rāma;
kṣatriyas who wage battle and do not flee even in conflict,

turning away from others' wives, others' wealth, and malice toward others;
vaiśyas whose auspicious livelihood is usury, agriculture, trade, and the like,

ever finding delight in the lotus feet of Raghunātha;
śūdras whose days and nights pass in serving brāhmaṇas,

and who utter ‘Rāma, Rāma’ on the tips of their tongues.
None of the common people there commit sin even in mind;

charity, compassion, self-restraint, and truth abide there constantly.
No sinless man speaks words that afflict others;

they feel no greed for another's wealth, nor do they commit evil.
In this manner, O great king, the subjects were ruled by Ratnagrīva.

Free from greed, he took the sixth share there and nothing else.
As the king was thus ruling his subjects according to dharma,

delighting in all pleasures, many years passed.
Once, O great king, he said this to [his wife] Viśālākṣī,

his devoted and lawful wife, wholly dedicated to fidelity:
‘O large-eyed one, sons have been born, capable of shouldering the protection of the subjects;

I have a large retinue, free from all anxiety;
my elephants are like mountains, my horses like the wind,

and my chariots yoked with fine horses are ever present.
By the grace of Mahāviṣṇu, I lack nothing.

Yet one desire remains in my mind:
I have not yet visited a supreme holy place, O exceedingly fair one,

adorned by Govinda, capable of ending residence in the womb.
I have now become old, with wrinkles and grey hair on my body;

reverently, I shall undertake the charming attendance upon a sacred place.
The man who, until the end of his life, only fills his own belly

and does not worship Hari, is regarded as a bull.
Therefore, O noble lady, dear one, I shall set out on a pilgrimage to a holy place,

with my family, having placed the burden of the kingdom securely on my son.’
Having so resolved, meditating on Hari at twilight in the course of the night,

he saw a dream of an excellent ascetic brāhmaṇa.
Rising at dawn, having performed his twilight rites and other rituals,

the great king sat comfortably in his assembly together with his ministers.
Just then he saw a brāhmaṇa ascetic with an emaciated body,

bearing matted locks, bark garments, and a loincloth, with a staff in hand,
his body sanctified through visits to many holy places.

Seeing him, the mighty-armed king bowed his head in reverence;
with a joyful heart, the king offered water for hospitality, foot-washing, and the like.

When the learned twice-born was comfortably seated and rested, he asked him:
‘Master, by the sight of you today the sin of my body is gone.

The great go respectfully to the homes of the wretched to protect them;
therefore tell me, O brāhmaṇa, now that I am old,

which deity, and which holy place would be capable of ending rebirth in the womb?
You are the foremost, omnipresent ones, intent on meditation and absorption,

pure, your souls sanctified by bathing in all sacred waters.
Explain in full, as it truly is, to me who am listening with faith,

by your grace, O you who are expert in all holy places!’
The brāhmaṇa said:
‘Listen, O chief of kings; I shall speak of the attendance on holy places about which you asked,

and by the grace of which deity ending rebirth in the womb takes place.
That glorious Rāmacandra, destroyer of the fever of transmigration, should be served;

that Lord named Puruṣottama is the one to be worshipped.
Various cities destroying all sins have been seen by me:

Ayodhyā, Sarayū, Tāpī, and Haridvāra, the supreme;
Avantī, pure Kāñcī, and the Revā flowing into the ocean;

Gokarṇa, and the one named Hāṭaka, which destroys millions of killings;
the great mountain called Mallika, which grants liberation to the men who behold it,

where water on the limbs of men becomes dark or pure—
this holy place, destroyer of sin, has indeed been seen by me.

Dvāravatī has been seen by me, frequented by gods and asuras,
where the Gomatī flows, auspicious, whose waters are directly Brahman;

where sleep is said to be dissolution and death is liberation, according to śruti;
in which Kali has no power at any time over men residing there;

where stones are marked with wheels, and human beings also bear the discus,
and beasts, insects, birds, and the like all have discus-marked bodies;

in which Trivikrama, the sole protector of all the worlds, dwells.
That city was brought within my range of sight through great merits.

Kurukṣetra was seen by me, which dispels all slaughter,
where Syamantapañcaka is, which destroys great sins.

Vārāṇasī was seen by me, where Viśvanātha has made his abode,
where the saving mantra named Brahman is taught;

casting aside the pleasure of enjoying their own actions,
go, free from sorrow, to Kailāsa;

where the holy place Maṇikarṇī is, in which the northward-flowing [Gaṅgā]
severs the bond of transmigration even for wrongdoers.
Wearing matted locks, earrings, and adorned with snakes, the foremost ones, / clad in elephant-hides, dwell freed from suffering.
Kālabhairava by name exercises Yama's punishment here; / the lord Yama, the wielder of the staff, enters into no report of men here.
Such was Kāśī, marked by Viśveśvara, seen by me. / Many other holy places too were seen by me, O protector of the earth.
Yet one great wonder was seen upon the Nīla Mountain, / in the presence of Puruṣottama, which was nowhere else visible to the eyes.

5.18.m: The Brahmin said: / Hear, O King, what took place on the best of mountains, Nīla, / through faith in which men attain the eternal absolute.
Wandering about, I went there to the mountain called Nīla, / whose courtyard is repeatedly washed by the waters of Gaṅgāsāgara.
There I saw Bhillas bearing bows upon the mountain summit, / four-armed, their fatigue dispelled by edible roots and fruits.
Then a very great doubt quickly arose in my mind: / "How is it that these men bearing bows and arrows are indeed four-armed?
The form of the self-controlled dwellers of Vaikuṇṭha is visible [here]; / how was this attained by them, which is difficult even for Brahmā and the others to obtain?
Their hands shine with the conch, discus, mace, bow, and lotus, / their bodies encircled by woodland garlands, like devotees of Viṣṇu right nearby."
With a mind overwhelmed by doubt, I then asked, O King: / "Who are you indeed, and how was this four-armed state obtained by you?"
Then, having laughed much, they replied to me: / "This Brahmin does not know the wondrous glorification of the food offering!"
"Hearing this, I too said: 'What pinda is given, and to whom? / Tell me that, O righteous beings who possess four-armed bodies!'"
Then, having heard my words, everything that had happened there— / the origin of their four-armed state and the rest—was related by those great-souled ones.
The Kirātas said: / "Listen, O Brahmin, to our account: a young boy of ours, / roaming playfully every day, eating rose-apples and other fruits,
once, while playing, climbed a delightful mountain peak, / surrounded on all sides by other children.
Then he saw there a wondrous temple of the god, / studded with emeralds and other jewels, having golden walls,
violently dispelling arrays of darkness with its own radiance like the sun. / Having seen it, he was filled with wonder: 'What is this? Whose house is this?
I will go and see what abode of great beings this is.' / Having reflected thus, he entered into the dwelling out of great good fortune.
There he saw the Lord of gods, bowed to by gods and asuras, / radiant with a diadem, necklace, armlets, neck-ornaments, and other gems,
wearing two delightful and extremely pure ear-ornaments, / with bees intoxicated by the fragrance of tulasī at His lotus feet,
His feet attended by the conch, discus, mace, bow, lotus, and other embodied [attributes], / that glorious form well-served by Nārada and the rest.
Some were singing, dancing, laughing most wonderfully, / pleasing that great King, praised by all worlds alone.
Having seen Hari, our boy went there, O sage. / The gods there, having performed an exalted worship equipped with incense and other rites,
having offered the food oblation for the beloved of Śrī, and then the waving of lights, / went each to their own home, O King, gazing with reverence upon His mercy.
Through the power of great fortune, a morsel of the fallen food offering was obtained by him, / which is difficult to attain even by Brahmā, the gods, suras, or men.
And having eaten that, and having gazed upon the glorious form, / the state of being four-armed was indeed attained by that handsome boy.
Then that boy, having returned home, was repeatedly observed by us / as having attained the state of being four-armed, holding the conch, discus, and other emblems.
He was asked by us: 'What wondrous thing is this that has happened?' / Then the boy told all of us that supreme wonder:
'I went earlier to the top of the peak, and there the Lord of gods was seen. / There a delightful morsel of the food offering was obtained by me.
Now, by the mere cause of eating it, / I have attained the state of being four-armed, filled with wonder.'
Hearing that speech of his, filled instantly with wonder, / that god, most difficult to attain, was also seen by us.
"Food and other offerings endowed with every taste were eaten there. / By the grace of the god we became four-armed once again. / Go there, best of men, and behold the god yourself.
And having eaten a morsel of food there, you too will become four-armed, O Brahmin. / That wonder which was asked by you has been told, O bull among Brahmins."

5.19.m: The Brahmin said: / "Having thus heard that wondrous speech of the Bhillas, / I considered this a great miracle and became exceedingly glad.
Having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, my body purified, / I climbed the peak there, variegated with gems and rubies.
There I saw, O great King, the God praised by the gods and others; / having bowed down and by partaking of the food, I became fulfilled.
I attained the four-armed state marked with the conch, discus, and other emblems; / by the sight of Puruṣottama, I shall not enter a womb again.
You too, O King, go quickly to that mountain called Nīla, / and make yourself fulfilled, freed from the sorrow of the womb."
Hearing this speech of that wise and foremost brāhmaṇa, / he, his body thrilled with joy, questioned the sage about the rules of pilgrimage.
The King said: / "Well said, O best of Brahmins, O virtuous one! You have spoken to me, O sinless one, / the glorification of Puruṣottama, which destroys sins for those who hear it.
Speak to me of that procedure for pilgrimage conforming to the Vedic revelation, / through which procedure men may attain the complete fruit."
The Brahmin said: / "Listen, O King, I shall proclaim the auspicious procedure for pilgrimage / by which the God bowed to by gods and asuras is attained.
Whether one's body has wrinkles and grey hair, or whether one is endowed with youth, / knowing death to be unavoidable, one should take refuge in Hari.
In praising Him, in hearing of Him, in paying homage to Him, and in worshipping Him / one's mind alone should be placed—not elsewhere, upon women and the like.
Seeing that everything is perishable, lasting only for a moment, and producing great grief, / [one should seek] Acyuta, who is beyond birth, death, and old age, and dear to devotion.
Even if a man worships [Him] somehow or other out of anger, desire, fear, hatred, / greed, or deceit, he does not experience distress.
That Hari arises from the company of the virtuous, which is devoid of sin, / by whose grace men become freed from misfortune.
Those virtuous ones, their passions calmed, free from desire and greed, / whatever they speak, O great King, turns one away from worldly existence.
In holy places, a virtuous person devoted to Rāmacandra is found, / the sight of whom is a fire that burns the heap of human sins.
Therefore, men fearful of worldly existence must go to holy places, / to sacred waters that are constantly adorned with rows of virtuous people.
Those holy places, when visited according to the rules, destroy sin. / O tiger among kings, bring that procedure within the reach of your hearing.
First, one should produce detachment regarding wife and household, / and knowing it to be unreal, remember Hari in one's mind.
Going merely one krośa away, constantly chanting 'Rāma, Rāma', / bathing there in holy waters and the like, one who knows the rule should shave his head.
For the sins of men who set out toward holy places / remain lodged in their hair; therefore, one should undergo tonsure.
Then, free from greed, wearing the attire of a pilgrim, / a man should take a knotless staff, a water pot, and an antelope skin.
Men who go according to rule obtain fruits pre-eminently; / therefore, with every effort, one should observe the rule of pilgrimage.
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well controlled, / and who possesses learning, asceticism, and fame, enjoys the fruit of the holy place.
'O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa! O Hari, O Kṛṣṇa! O lover of your devotees, O Lord of cows! / O refuge, O Lord Viṣṇu, save me from the vast cycle of rebirth!'
Speaking thus with his tongue and remembering Hari in his mind, / the fortunate man should travel on foot toward the holy place.
A man going by vehicle obtains only half the fruit, / with shoes a fourth part; and by a cow-drawn cart, [he incurs the sin of] cow-slaughter and the like.
A trader [obtains] a third share; by serving [others], he gets an eighth share; / going unwillingly to the holy place, one obtains half the fruit.
Just as the pilgrimage to sacred sites is properly performed, / the destruction of sins surely occurs, especially through observing the rule.
There one should bow down to the virtuous with salutations and acts of service at their feet; / through that, indeed, devotion to Hari is attained in Puruṣottama.
Thus the rule of pilgrimage has been told in brief, not in full detail; / adopting such a rule, go to Puruṣottama.
Pleased with you, O great king, Acyuta will grant you devotion, / through which the termination of worldly existence will take place in an instant.
Hearing the rule for pilgrimage, which destroys all sins, / one is freed from all fierce sins, O bull among men.
Sumati said: / Having heard this speech, the great king bowed to his feet, / his mind overwhelmed with longing to see that holy place.
Resolving to take everyone along through his desire for pilgrimage, / he ordered his foremost minister, who was most skilled in counsel:
"Instruct the ministers and all the citizens by my command, / for the sake of the joy of beholding the lotus feet of Puruṣottama:
'Whoever are people in my city and do my bidding, / let all those excellent men depart from my city along with me.
Those men who transgress my word and remain at home / are to be punished with Yama's punishment, as sinners and causes of unrighteousness.
What use is that multitude of sons, or what use are ill-behaved kinsmen, / by whom Puruṣottama, the giver of merit, has not been seen with their own eyes?
Their birth is like that of a herd of swine that eat excrement, / whose sons or grandsons have not taken refuge in Hari.
Quickly bow to that God who is able to purify all by His name alone, / O multitudes of my subjects!'"
At these charming words, woven with the virtues of the Lord, / the prime minister, the noble one named Satya, rejoiced greatly.
Mounting an excellent elephant, he proclaimed with a drum / what was commanded here by the king who desired the pilgrimage:
"Let the people quickly go with the king to the great mountain; / let the destroyer of sins, named Puruṣottama, be seen!
Let the entire ocean of worldly existence be made like a cow's footprint; / let men adorn their bodies with marks such as the conch and discus!"
The minister, whose fatigue was dispelled by meditation on the feet of the lord of the Raghus, / proclaimed all such wondrous things as had been ordered by the king.
Hearing that, all those subjects, flooded with the essence of bliss, / set their minds on their own deliverance through the sight of Puruṣottama.
There the brāhmaṇas set forth well-attired with their disciples, / bestowing blessings rich with the granting of boons upon the king.
Heroic kṣatriyas bearing bows, vaiśyas endowed with goods for trade, / and śūdras, their bodies thrilled with joy at the deliverance from worldly existence;
washermen, leather-workers, artisans, hunters, builders of walls, / those living by tailoring, and traders in betel;
those holding rhythm instruments, those living by the stage, / sellers of oil, and sellers of cloth;
sūtas reciting Purāṇic lore filled with joy, / Māgadhas, and bards went forth at the king's command;
those living by medical practice, those skilled at dice, / connoisseurs of the tastes of cooked foods, entertainers with humorous words,
practitioners of the magical arts, and those well-versed in news, / departed from the midst of the city praising the great king.
The king also, having performed there the morning rites and rituals, / brought the pure brāhmaṇa, the foremost of ascetics.
By his command, the great king departed outside the city; / followed by the people, the king shone like the moon with the stars.
Having gone merely one krośa, he then shaved his head according to the rule; / holding a staff, a water pot, and an auspicious deer skin,
endowed with an auspicious guise, intent on meditating upon Hari, / the highly renowned king kept his mind free from desire, anger, and the like.
Then kettledrums, bherī-drums, ānakas, paṇavas, / and conches, vīṇās, and other instruments were repeatedly sounded by their players.
"Victory, O Lord of gods, O destroyer of sorrow, known as Puruṣottama! / Reveal your form to me!" saying this, the people went forth.

5.20.m: Sumati said: / Then, when the ruler of the earth had departed accompanied by all the people, / the chanting of Kṛṣṇa's praise was performed by great Vaiṣṇavas and singers.
That great king heard on the road the chanting of Govinda: / "Victory, O Mādhava, refuge of devotees, O Puruṣottama!"
Visiting many holy sites along the way and seeing their great glory, / he then heard their majesty from the ascetic brāhmaṇa.
With his mind entertained by various narrations of Viṣṇu, the king / had singers sing of Mahāviṣṇu at every stretch of the road.
To the poor, the blind, the destitute, and the lame, the wise king, / having mastered his senses, gave gifts suited for their maintenance.
Purifying himself in numerous holy places and attaining auspiciousness, / he proceeded with his people, intent on meditating on Hari.
As he went, the king saw ahead a river that destroys sins, / filled with stones marked with the discus, as pure as the minds of sages,
adorned with many rows of crowds of sages, / and graced by the calls of cranes and other birds.
Seeing it, he asked that foremost ascetic brāhmaṇa, who knew dharma / and was rich with knowledge of the distinct glories of many holy sites:
"O master, what is this sacred river, frequented by hosts of sages, / that fills my heart with an abundance of extreme joy?"
Hearing that speech of that wise king of kings, / the learned one began to relate the supreme glorification of the holy place.

The brāhmaṇa said:
This river Gaṇḍakī, O king, is frequented by gods and asuras; / with its stream of holy water, it destroys heaps of sins.
By beholding [it], one burns mental sin; by touching [it], sin born of actions; / [and] by drinking its water, one burns the mass of verbal sins.
In ancient times, the lord of creatures, seeing all creatures impure, / created this [river] from drops of his cheek to destroy numerous sins.
Those men who touch this river of holy water, having beautiful waves, / never enter a womb [again], even if they have committed sins.
And the stones born in it that are adorned with wheel marks— / they are indeed the Supreme Lord manifest, bearing His own transcendental form.
A man who daily worships a stone marked with a wheel / shall never again enter a mother's womb.
The wise man who worships the excellent śālagrāma stone / should be of good conduct, devoid of hypocrisy and greed.
By a man averse to another's wife and another's wealth / the śālagrāma marked with a wheel must indeed be worshiped with effort.
The wheel born in Dvāravatī and the stone born in the Gaṇḍakī / take away instantly a man's sins acquired in hundreds of births.
Even if a man has committed thousands of sins, / by drinking water [washed over] a śālagrāma stone he becomes pure in an instant.
A householder—whether a brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, or a śūdra abiding by the Vedic path— / attains liberation by worshiping a śālagrāma.
Never should worship of a śālagrāma be performed by a woman, / [whether] husbandless or fortunate, seeking the benefit of the heavenly realm.
A woman who out of delusion touches [it], even if endowed with good birth and virtuous conduct, / loses her store of merit and swiftly goes to hell.
Flowers dropped from a woman's hand upon a śālagrāma stone / fall with greater impact than a thunderbolt, the best of brāhmaṇas declare.
Sandalpaste [offered by her] becomes like poison, a flower like a thunderbolt, / [and] an offering of food made to the Lord becomes like the kālakūṭa poison.
Therefore, a woman must avoid touching the stone by all means; / she who does so goes to hell for as long as fourteen Indras rule.
Even one of sinful conduct, or even one tainted by the murder of a brāhmaṇa, / goes to the highest destination after drinking water [washed over] a śālagrāma stone.
Tulasī, sandalpaste, water, a conch, a bell, and a wheel, / a stone, a copper vessel, the name of Viṣṇu, and the nectar of [His] feet—
The calm sages, conversant with the meaning of all scriptures, say / that the nectar of His feet, together with these nine, burns away a heap of sins.
Whatever merit arises from bathing at every sacred bath and from worshiping at every sacrifice, / that wonderful [merit] is present, O king, in every single drop.
Wherever a śālagrāma stone is worshiped by the best of men, / within a single yojana of that place are present crores of sacred baths.
Śālagrāmas are to be worshiped in even numbers, but not a pair among even [numbers]; / they may indeed be worshiped in odd numbers, but not three among odd [numbers].
Where there is the union of both the wheel born in Dvāravatī / and that born in the Gaṇḍakī, there is the Gaṅgā flowing to the sea.
Rough [stones] deprive men of lifespan, fortune, and strength; / therefore smooth ones of captivating form bestow fortune.
A man who desires long life or a man who desires wealth / obtains everything, both otherworldly and earthly, by worshiping [them].
At the moment of death, a fortunate man, O king, / has the holy name of Hari on his lips and the stone near his heart.
Even if through faith the image of the śālagrāma stone manifests / while his breaths are departing, he without doubt attains liberation.
In ancient times it was spoken by the Lord to the wise Ambarīṣa: / 'Brāhmaṇas, gentle ascetics, and śālagrāma stones—
this threefold form of mine has indeed been assumed on the surface of the earth / by me rising up to remove the sins of sinners.
Those sinners who insult the śālagrāma stone even once / are cooked at once in the Kumbhīpāka [hell] until the dissolution of all beings.
That fool who prevents one who has undertaken to perform its worship— / his mother, father, and circle of kinsmen become share-holders in hell.
Or whoever speaks what is dear, [saying], “Perform the worship of śālagrāma,” / achieves his purpose and swiftly leads his ancestors to Vaikuṇṭha.'
On this very subject, sages free from passion / and devoid of desire and anger cite this ancient legendary history.
Long ago, in the region called Kīkaṭa, which was devoid of dharma, / there was an outcaste man of the Pulkasa caste named Śabara.
Constantly intent on slaughtering creatures, holding a bow again and again, / he violently took the lives of those wishing to go to a sacred bath.
Perpetrator of the slaughter of many living beings, always devoted to others' wealth, / he was ever bound by attachment and the like, full of passion, anger, and so forth.
Wandering day and night in the dread forest, committing the slaughter of creatures, / he was formidable with his drawn bowstring and arrows tipped with poison.
Wandering once, that hunter who caused terror to all living beings, / cruel-minded as he was, did not realize that death had arrived nearby.
The messengers of Yama arrived, with nooses and clubs in their hands, / copper-haired, with long claws and protruding fangs, terrifying,
dark, bearing iron shackles, causing stupefaction, / [saying]: 'Bind this sinner who terrifies all living beings!
Never even in thought did he benefit any living being, / devoted to another's wife, another's wealth, and malice toward others.

Therefore I shall pull out his huge tongue!' / And one said: 'I shall tear out his eyes!'

One said: 'I shall cut off both hands of this sinner!' / Another said: 'I shall sever the ears of this wicked soul!'
Speaking thus intensely, grinding teeth against teeth, / those furious ones, armed with weapons, approached and stood before that wicked soul.
Then one messenger assumed the form of a serpent and bit him on the foot; / as soon as he was bitten, he suddenly died.
Then those servants of Yama bound him with an iron noose, / flogged him with whips, and struck him with clubs in wrath:
'O wicked, vile-hearted soul! You never performed good deeds / even in thought; therefore we shall cast you into the Raurava hells!
Ferocious crows will devour your skin and flesh in anger; / from your birth onward, you never served Hari!
By doing harm you nourished your wife, sons, and the rest; / never did you remember the god Janārdana, who removes sin!
Therefore, by the command of Dharmarāja, we shall take you / to an iron stake, to Kumbhīpāka, and to Raurava, with many blows!'
When Yama's servants, having spoken thus, were about to lead him away, / just then arrived [a sage] devoted to the lotus feet of Mahāviṣṇu.
Then the noble Vaiṣṇava saw the messengers of Yama, / hordes bearing evil weapons such as nooses, clubs, and rods,
having bound the Pulkasa with iron shackles and preparing to go, / crying: 'Bind, bind! Seize! Cut! Pierce, pierce!'
Then, seeing him, the compassionate one, devoted to Padmanābha, / directed his heart toward him with immense compassion.
[He thought:] 'Let him not suffer severe torture in my presence! / I shall release him this very day from the messengers of Yama!'
Making up his mind thus toward him, the lord of sages, filled with compassion, / took a Śālagrāma stone in his hand and approached him.
Pouring into his mouth the holy foot-washing water mixed with tulasī leaves, / he whispered the name of Rāma into his ear.
The Vaiṣṇava placed tulasī upon his head; / placing the stone of Mahāviṣṇu on his heart, that Vaiṣṇava said:
"Let the messengers of Yama, intent upon tortures, depart! / May the touch of the śālagrāma stone consume his great sin!"
As he spoke thus, the wondrous attendants of Viṣṇu / arrived near him, whose sins were removed by the touch of the stone.
Wearing yellow garments, adorned with conch, discus, mace, and lotus, / they came and released him from the dreadful iron noose.
Having released the Pulkasa man, the committer of great sins, / they asked, "Why was this Vaiṣṇava, who bears a venerable body, bound?
Whose orders do you carry out, that you perform such adharma? / Release this Vaiṣṇava! Why indeed has he been held?"
Hearing this speech, the servants of Yama spoke, / who had arrived by order of Dharmarāja, intent on carrying off the sinner.
He never once even in thought helped any living being; / a slaughterer of creatures, a committer of great sins, bearing a wicked body.
He robbed many people travelling on pilgrimages; / always devoted to others' wives, the agent of every sin.
Therefore we have come to carry away this sinful Pulkasa man. / Why has he been freed by you warriors, who have arrived all of a sudden?"
The messengers of Viṣṇu said: / "Sins such as killing a brāhmaṇa, arising from the slaughter of ten million living beings— / the touch of a śālagrāma stone consumes all of it in an instant.
If the name 'Rāma' enters one's ear even by chance, / it causes the burning of sin, just as a spark of fire burns cotton.
He on whose head is tulasī, on whose heart is the charming stone, / or in whose mouth or ear is the name of Rāma—he is liberated that very moment.
Therefore, tulasī was placed on his head just now, / the name of Rāma was immediately made heard, and the stone was well held on his heart.
Hence his multitude of sins has been burned away; his body has become pure. / He will go to the supreme abode, which is exceedingly difficult for sinners to attain.
Having enjoyed all delightful pleasures there for ten thousand years, / and then taking birth in Bhārata and worshipping the Teacher of the World,
he will attain the supreme state, exceedingly difficult even for gods and asuras to reach. / The greatness of the stone of the Supreme Lord has not been properly understood;
seen, touched, or worshipped, it removes all sins in an instant." / Having spoken thus, all the attendants of Mahāviṣṇu ceased with joy.
Those servants of Yama related the wonder to their king. / The Vaiṣṇava, devoted to the Lord of the Raghus, experienced great delight.
He was freed from the noose of Yama and went to the supreme abode. / Then there arrived a spotless aerial chariot, adorned with a network of tiny bells,
charming and wondrous, coming from the realm of the gods. / Having mounted it, he went to heaven, frequented by those of great merit.
Having enjoyed abundant pleasures, he returned to the earth. / Attaining a birth in Kāśī in an upright and noble brāhmaṇa family,
and worshipping the Lord of the Worlds, he went to the supreme abode. / That sinner, through the company of the virtuous and by touching the śālagrāma stone,
was completely freed from great suffering and went to the supreme abode. / I have told you, O king, this great account of the Gaṇḍakī;
hearing it, one is freed from sins, and obtains both enjoyment and liberation.

5.21.m: Sumati said: / Having brought this peerless glorification of the Gaṇḍakī to the range of his ears, / that best of kings considered himself fulfilled.
Bathing in the holy site and thoroughly gratifying all his ancestors, the great [king] rejoiced, / performing worship of the śālagrāma stones according to the words of the brāhmaṇa.
Taking twenty-four stones there, that best of kings / worshipped them with devotion using sandal paste and other offerings.
Having distributed gifts there, especially to the poor and the blind, / the king set out to go to the abode of Puruṣottama.
Thus, in due course, he reached the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. / Bringing it into view, he joyfully asked a brāhmaṇa:
"O master, tell me: how far is the great mountain named Nīla, / the dwelling of Puruṣottama, bowed to by gods and asuras?"
Hearing these weighty words of King Ratnagrīva, / he, filled with astonishment, respectfully spoke to the king:
"O king, this very place of the Nīla mountain is revered! / Why is it not seen at all, though it bestows the fruit of great merit?"
Again and again he said, "This is the site of the Nīla mountain! / Why is it not seen, O king, the abode of Puruṣottama?
I bathed well here; here the Bhillas were visible to my eyes; / and by this very path, O king, the top of the mountain was ascended!"
Hearing his words, the king was grieved in his heart, / making his mind eager to behold the Blue Mountain.
He said: "Then how, O brāhmaṇa, can Puruṣottama be seen? / Or how can the Nīla mountain be seen? Tell us the means for that!"
Hearing those words of King Ratnagrīva, / the ascetic brāhmaṇa, amazed at the king, said:
"Having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, O lord of the earth, / we must remain right here as long as the Nīla mountain is not seen.
The god named Puruṣottama is sung of as the destroyer of sins; / he who bears the name 'compassionate to his devotees' will soon show grace.
That crest-jewel of the gods does not abandon his devotees; / many devotees have been protected by him. Therefore sing of him, O noble-minded one!"
Hearing these words with an afflicted mind, the king / bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, and then began fasting.
"When Puruṣottama shows grace with his vision, / then, having worshipped him, I shall eat; otherwise, fasting is my vow."
Having thus undertaken the observance on the shore of the Gaṅgā-sāgara, / he then observed the fast, singing the host of Hari's virtues.

The king said: / "Victory, O Lord who shows mercy to the distressed! Victory, O remover of sorrow whose very name is auspicious! / Victory, O assumed embodiment who destroys the suffering of devotees! Victory, O slayer of the wicked!
Seeing Ambarīṣa distressed, all his auspicious fortune destroyed by the brāhmaṇa's curse, / holding the Sudarśana discus in your own hand, you protected him from dwelling in a womb.

When he was caused distress by his father, the king of Daityas, with tridents, nooses, water, and throwing into fire, / you, assuming the form of glorious Nṛsiṃha, instantly protected him while his father looked on.
Seeing the mighty lord of elephants fallen into the jaws of a crocodile, tormented by intense agony, / your mind truly melting with compassion, you mounted Garuḍa;

leaving the lord of birds, wielding your discus, your garlands and garments trembling from the speed, / you are praised by the noble as the one who instantly freed him from the crocodile and destroyed it.
Wherever there is distress for your servant, there indeed, O Lord, assuming a body, / you protect your own by means of charming deeds that remove sins.
O Lord of the destitute! O beloved of devotees, whose soles are rubbed by the diamonds in the crests of the gods! / O Lord who burns ten million sins, reveal your sight to me!
If it comes to your mind that this person is a sinner, even so, grant your vision! / We are yours, O destroyer of the flood of sins, worshipped by gods and asuras; we are not forgotten!"
"Those who speak your spotless name cross the ocean of all sins. / If recollection has been made by me, then may it be obtained, O dispeller of all suffering!"
Sumati said: / Thus singing [his] virtues by night or by day, the ruler of the earth / did not rest even for a moment; nor did he attain sleep or comfort.
Singing as he walked, praising as he stood, day and night he said this: / "Reveal your own form, O Lord of mercy, O Puruṣottama!"
Thus five days passed for the king at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. / Then the ocean of mercy, the lord of cows, thought out of compassion:
"This king, freed from sin through singing of me, / may behold my most beloved [form], bowed down to by gods and asuras."
Considering this, the blessed lord, his mind filled with compassion, / assumed the guise of an ascetic and went near the king, all-powerful.
Going there, O great king, wearing the garb of a triple-staffed ascetic, / arrived out of compassion for his devotee, he was indeed seen by the ascetic [brahmin].
Saying, "Homage to Viṣṇu!", the best of kings bowed down; / having his mind set on Hari, he performed worship with water for guest-offering, water for the feet, and a seat.
He said: "Incomparable is my good fortune that you are visible to the eyes! / Henceforth Govinda will grant me the sight of himself."
Hearing those words of his, the ascetic spoke to him: / "O king, listen to the words uttered from my mouth!"
Through knowledge I know what has been, what is to be, and what is happening. / Therefore I speak a little; listen with a single-pointed mind!
Tomorrow at midday Hari will grant a vision hard even for Brahmā to attain. / Along with five of your own people, you will go to the supreme abode:
you, the minister, your wife, the ascetic brahmin, / and previously in your city, the pious weaver named Karamba.
With these five, on this best of mountains, Nīla, / you will go to that which is praised by Brahmā and Devendra, and worshipped by the gods."
Having spoken thus, the ascetic vanished from sight and was seen nowhere; / hearing that, the king experienced joy together with amazement.
The king said: / "O master, who was this ascetic that came and spoke to me? / He is not seen again; where has he gone, the giver of joy to the heart?"
The ascetic said: / "O king, his mind drawn by your great love, he came here— / he named Puruṣottama, the destroyer of all sins.
Tomorrow at midday a great mountain will appear before you. / Having climbed it and seen Hari, you will have accomplished your goal."
His inner fever dispelled by the flood of nectar from those words, / the king attained a joy that even Brahmā does not know.
Then kettledrums resounded, along with vīṇās, drums, and horns. / Great bliss then indeed arose in the heart of the king of kings.
Singing Hari, pausing for a moment, laughing, talking, speaking, bowing, / he attained profound bliss, the destroyer of all torment.

5.22.m: Sumati said: / Then, having spent the entire day in remembrances and praises of Hari, / he slept at night on the bank of the Gaṅgā, which yields great fruit.

In a dream, however, he saw himself four-armed, / bearing a conch, discus, mace, lotus, and the bow Śārṅga;

[He saw Him] dancing before Puruṣottama together with Śarva and the other gods, / accompanied by their splendid embodiments, holding the disc, mace, water-born lotus, weapons, and others.

seeing the Lord of Śrī constantly worshipped by hosts of excellent attendants headed by Viṣvaksena, endowed with beautiful bodies, / he experienced extraordinary wonder regarding that realm and an exceedingly marvellous joy;
and the wise [king] considered himself a recipient of mercy / from the one named Puruṣottama, who grants the heart's desire.
Having seen such a vision in a dream, that best of kings, / awake at dawn, told the brāhmaṇa the dream he had beheld.
Hearing that, the wise brahmin said with amazement: / "O king, that one named Puruṣottama who was seen by you,
Hari will give [you] his own form marked with conch, discus, and other [attributes]." / Hearing his words, the noble-minded Ratnagrīva
caused gifts to be given according to the wish of the poor. / Having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, and having gratified the ancestors and gods,
singing the host of Hari's virtues, he awaited his vision. / Then at midday, in the sky, drums repeatedly
struck by the hands of the gods sounded with many sounds. / And suddenly a shower of flowers fell upon the king's head.
"Blessed are you, O best of kings! Behold Nīla visible to your eyes!"
When the king heard these words prompted by the gods, / then that wonderful [peak], bearing splendour greater than millions of suns,
the great mountain named Nīla, became visible to the king's eyes, / resplendent all around with peaks of silver and gold.
"Is this fire blazing, or is it a second sun? / Or is this an unexpected mass of lightning possessing a steady brilliance?"
Seeing the beautifully adorned tableland of Nīla, the ascetic brahmin / announced to the king: "This is the holy great mountain."
Hearing that, the best of kings bowed with his head: / "I am blessed, I have attained my purpose; Nīla has come within the range of my sight!"
The minister, the king's wife, and Karamba the weaver / became overjoyed at the sight of Nīla, O bull among men.
These five climbed Mount Nīla at the auspicious hour of victory, / hearing the sounds of the great drums made by the immortals.
On its upper peak, adorned with wondrous trees, / he saw an unsurpassed temple of the Lord, overlaid with gold,
where Brahmā, arriving, always performs the worship of the Supreme Lord, / [and] where he offers food offerings that cause Hari's delight.
Then, seeing that spotless, supreme abode of God, / he entered, surrounded by his five companions.
Seeing there, seated on a throne of gold / decorated with great jewels, the captivating four-armed [Lord],
served by Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, Vijaya, Jaya, and others, / the king bowed down along with his wife and servants.
Having bowed to the Supreme Self, the best of gods, the great king / bathed him according to rule with bathing mantras spoken in the Veda.
With a pleased heart, the king offered guest-water, foot-water, and the like; / having anointed him with sandalwood and presented him with fine clothes,
and having offered incense and the waving of lights, the king then offered / to the divine image a food offering that was delightful with all [kinds of] flavours.
Having bowed down, he and the ascetic brahmin praised [him] / according to their capacity with collections of hymns strung together from the multitude of his virtues.
The king said: / "You alone are the supreme Person manifest, the Lord beyond material nature, / distinct from cause and effect, worshipped by the intellect-principle and the rest.
From the lotus of your navel was born Brahmā, skilled in creation, / and likewise Rudra, the agent of destruction, was born from your eye.
Commanded by you, he carries out the activity of this universe. / From you, the ancient beginning, was born the world, both motionless and moving."

Pervading consciousness with your power, ah, you make this [world] conscious! / You indeed have no birth, nor any end, O Lord of the world. / There are no growth, decay, or transformations in you, O omnipresent Lord!
Nevertheless, for the protection of devotees and to establish dharma, / you undertake births and deeds, and assume corresponding qualities.
Taking the form of the Fish, you slew the demon Śaṅkha, / and the Vedas were well protected, O Brahman, O supreme Being, O firstborn!
Even Śeṣa does not know your greatness, nor does the great goddess Bhāratī; / how much less others like me, O Mahāviṣṇu, who possess base intellects?
Even this supreme speech, along with the mind, does not attain you; / therefore, how could I be able to praise you, O Lord?
Having thus praised Him, he bowed down repeatedly with his head, / his voice choked with emotion and his limbs marked with horripilation.
Rejoicing in his heart at this hymn of praise, the blessed Lord Puruṣottama / spoke true and meaningful words to the king.
The Blessed Lord said: / By your hymn, O king of great intellect, I have rejoiced! / Know me, O great king, to be beyond primordial matter.
Quickly partake of the charming food-offering! / Attaining a four-armed form, you shall go to the supreme abode.
The mortal who praises me with this jewel of a hymn composed by you, / to him also I will grant my sight, which bestows worldly enjoyment, liberation, and boons.
Having heard these words spoken by the Lord, the king / ate the food offering along with four servants.
Then an aerial chariot arrived, adorned with clusters of tiny bells, / served by hosts of Apsarases, and endowed with every enjoyment.
Beholding the one known as the Supreme Person, that righteous king, / having made himself a vessel of his grace, paid homage at his feet.
By his command, boarding the aerial chariot along with his wife, / he went to wondrous Vaikuṇṭha in heaven, before his very eyes.
The king's minister, devoted to dharma and the foremost knower of all duties, / went alongside in an aerial chariot, served by a host of lovely women.
The ascetic brāhmaṇa there, who had bathed in all sacred bathing places, / attained a four-armed form and went with the gods riding in aerial chariots.
Karamva also, O great king, by the merit of singing obtained the sight [of the Lord] / and went to the abode of the gods, difficult to attain even for all the gods and others.
All departed for the supreme, wondrous realm of Viṣṇu, / four-armed, holding the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
All had the splendor of dark clouds, pure, holding radiant lotuses in their hands, / and their bodies adorned with necklaces, armlets, and bracelets, they went to heaven.
Beholding those rows of aerial chariots, the roar of kettle drums / was then brought to the ears of the people and subjects.
Then there was a brāhmaṇa, devoted to the lotus feet of Viṣṇu, / who went, his heart drawn by separation from him, and became four-armed.
Seeing that wonder, those people, praising that great good fortune, / bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean and returned to the city.
Oh, the good fortune of the virtuous king Ratnagrīva! / In this very body he went to that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
O king, that is the Blue Mountain, consecrated by the Supreme Person; / by merely beholding it, they surely go to Vaikuṇṭha, the supreme haven.
He who hears this glorification of the Blue Mountain is fortunate; / he who recites it to the people—both will go to the supreme abode.
Upon hearing this, bad dreams are destroyed by mere remembrance; / at the end [of life], the Supreme Person grants crossing over the cycle of rebirth.
He who resides on the Blue Mountain is Rāma, the Supreme Person; / Sītā is directly Mahālakṣmī, the cause of all causes.
Having performed the horse sacrifice, he will surely purify the worlds; / whose name is prescribed as the expiation for slaying a brāhmaṇa.
Now your horse has reached the Blue Mountain, the best of mountains; / pay homage to the god, the Supreme Person, O wise one!
Becoming sinless there, we will go to the supreme abode; / by his grace, many have crossed over the ocean of cyclic existence.
As he was speaking thus, the horse reached the Blue Mountain, / pounding the surface of the earth with the speed of the wind.
Then the king, following behind it, reached the mountain named the Blue Mountain, / and having bathed at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, went to the Supreme Person.
Having praised and bowed to the Lord of gods, who is worshipped by gods and asuras, / that slayer of enemies considered himself to have achieved his purpose.

5.23.m: Śeṣa said: / Having stood for a moment and eaten grass, the horse, swift as thought, departed, / surrounded by ranks of warriors, bearing a message on its forehead, and accompanied by a chowrie.
It was protected by the great hero Śatrughna, by King Lakṣmīnidhi, / by Puṣkala, by Ugravāha, and by the foremost in valor.
It went to the city named Cakrāṅkā, protected by Subāhu, / guarded and followed by many millions of warriors, O Lord.
Then his mighty son Damana, engaged in hunting, / saw the horse with the scroll on its forehead, anointed with sandalwood paste and the like.
Having seen it, he said to a servant: "Whose horse has come into my sight? / What is this scroll worn on its forehead, and this beautiful chowrie?"
Hearing the king's words, the servant went from there / to where the handsome horse with a scroll upon its forehead was present.
Seizing it by its mane, adorned with a garland of jewels, / he led it before the prince of Subāhu's lineage.
He had the scroll read, which was adorned with beautiful letters: / "There was a powerful king, Daśaratha, the ruler of Ayodhyā.
His son is Rāmabhadra, the crest-jewel of all heroes; / there is none other equal to him on earth in the prowess of wielding the bow.
By him this horse, anointed with sandalwood and the like, has been loosed; / the righteous Śatrughna, slayer of enemy heroes, protects it.
And whatever warriors say, 'We are the heroes! Here we stand with bows in hand,' / let them seize by force this steed adorned with a garland of jewels.
And Śatrughna, the crest-jewel of all heroes, will release it; / otherwise, let the archers offer obeisance at his feet."
Perceiving this intention, the king's son spoke: / "Is Rāma alone the wielder of the bow, and are we not considered kṣatriyas?"
While my father stands on the earth, what is this great pride in the world? / Let him reap the fruit of his pride through arrows shot from my bow!
Today let my sharp arrows make Śatrughna like a blossoming kiṃśuka tree, / his body completely covered in wounds.
Let my arrows split the temples of their elephants, / and let them behold horses by the hundreds inundated in floods of blood.
Let hosts of Yoginīs drink blood from human skulls; / let female jackals be satisfied by devouring the flesh of my enemies.
Let his fine warriors behold the great strength of my arms, / as I release millions of arrows shot from the rod of my bow!"
Having spoken thus, the king's son named Damana, / having sent that [horse] to his own city, became delighted and fierce.
He said this to the commander of the army: "O wise one, prepare / a limited army for me to repel the host of enemies!"
Having quickly prepared his army, the fierce one stood facing [the enemy] on the battleground, / just as the followers of the horse arrived.
"Where is that horse of the great king, marked with the written plate on its forehead?" / Thus they asked one another, repeatedly and exceedingly agitated.
Then Pratāpāgrya, scorcher of foes, saw before him / the army arrayed, resounding with the shouts of heroes.
There some people said: "The horse was taken by this [prince], O king; / otherwise, how could this hero stand facing us, accompanied by his forces?"
