Hearing this, the exceedingly glorious one sent a servant; / he went there and asked: "Where is the horse of King Rāma?"
By whom has it been taken? Whence was it taken? Does the foolish-minded one not know Rāma, / to whom the gods headed by Śakra bowed down, presenting tribute?
Indeed, the mighty, enraged army of that Dharmarāja / will devour [him] utterly if he does not submit."
Hearing what was said, the mighty prince was deeply distressed, / and rebuked him with a stream of words:
"The sacrificial horse, adorned with the inscribed plate and other ornaments, was taken by me. / Let those who are heroes defeat me by force and release it from here!"
Hearing his words, the servant departed laughing, full of wrath, / and reported to the king exactly as it was described.
Hearing that, Pratāpāgrya of great might, his eyes copper-red with anger, / went forth to fight the prince, surrounded by great heroes,
in a chariot of golden parts, splendid with four horses, / having an excellent pole and filled with all weapons, the mighty one went forth.
Possessed of great might, he twanged his bow / and laughed loudly again and again, tears welling up from his rage.
Horse-riders and elephant-riders, with swords flashing in their hands, / followed Pratāpāgrya, their eyes agitated and filled with fury.
Elephants and foot-soldiers by the millions, ready for battle, / had long desired this combat brought about by the hero.
Recognizing that the enemy army was then ready, the prince, / foremost among heroes, went forth surrounded by a mighty force.
Prepared, armored, sword-bearing, and holding a bow, the youth / went to fight with effortless ease, like the king of beasts against a herd of elephants.
Then the enraged warriors, skilled in the work of battle, / sought to slay one another, shouting: "Cut! Pierce!"
Foot-soldiers clashed with a multitude of foot-soldiers, elephant-riders with horse-riders, / chariot-fighters with those stationed in chariots, and horsemen with those mounted on steeds.
Elephants were split in two, and horses were cut into halves; / the earth became filled with the brains of countless men.
Then King Pratāpāgrya of great might became enraged / upon seeing the prince engaged in slaughtering his army.
He said to his charioteer there: "Drive the horses to where / that prince, the great chariot-warrior, is intent on slaughtering my host."
Then the powerful prince, whose feet were bowed to by crest-jewels of heroes, / went directly to face Pratāpāgrya.
The charioteer drove Pratāpāgrya's horses / to where the heroic Damana was, the crest-jewel of all warriors.
Approaching him, he challenged that prince who was ready for battle; / standing in his chariot refined with gold and bearing the rod of his bow, [he said]:
"O prince! O child! By you the best of horses has been tied up; / you do not know the great king served by all the chiefs of heroes!
Whose wondrous majesty even the lord of Daityas was unable to endure— / taking his horse, you have entered your city!
Know me to have arrived before you, an enemy taking the form of Death! / Release the horse, child! Go at once and play with your toys!
Whose son are you? Where are you from? Why did you, shortsighted one, / capture the horse? Yet pity has arisen in me for you, O child!"
Hearing this, high-minded Damana smiled, / and, treating his army like a blade of grass, said to Pratāpāgrya:
Damana said: / "By force was the horse captured by me and taken to my own city; / while I have life, I shall not surrender it today! Fight, O mighty one!
As for what you said: 'You are a boy; go and play with your toys'— / watch that play of mine, O great king, at the forefront of the battle!
Śeṣa said: / Having spoken thus, the son of Subāhu strung his bow, / and aimed a hundred arrows at the chest of Pratāpāgrya.
Fitting a hundred arrows, the glorious one blew his conch; / at that sound of the conch, fear arose in the faint-hearted.
He struck [Pratāpāgrya] in the chest with a hundred arrows; / Pratāpāgrya, quick of hand, cut off those well-jointed [shafts].
Seeing the arrows cut down, the mighty prince was enraged / and discharged sharp broad-headed arrows fletched with heron feathers.
In the sky, on the earth, and in the space between, beautiful arrows were seen, / marked with his own name, splendid in their sharp falling stream.
The arrows, striking upon his arms and chest, / emitting numerous sparks of fire, burned the army; it was immense.
Pratāpāgrya, greatly enraged, shouted, "Halt! Halt!" / and struck him on the head with ten arrows.
Those arrows, fixed in the prince's forehead, / shone, O sage, like ten branches of a tree.
Under that impact of arrows, the high-minded prince was not shaken, / just as a seven-year-old elephant struck with a stick [is not].
Fitting three hundred splendid arrows to his bow, he released them, / decorated with golden shafts, resembling the fire of cosmic dissolution.
Those arrows, indeed, having pierced Pratāpāgrya's chest, went down, / smeared with blood, like people turned away from devotion to Rāmacandra.
Pratāpāgrya, enraged, releasing arrows by the thousands, / quickly deprived Subāhu's son of his chariot in that very instant.
With four [arrows] he brought down the four horses, with two the banner; / with one he threw down the charioteer's head from his body to the earth.
With four he struck that prince again, / and in that very moment, with one, he cut his bow along with the string.
Mounting another chariot adorned with jewel-like horses, / the high-minded [Damana] took a bow in hand and strung it.
He replied to Pratāpāgrya: "You have displayed wonderful prowess; / now behold the prowess of my bow, O good warrior!"
Having spoken thus, Damana took ten arrows; / with four he sent the four horses to Yama's abode.
With four the chariot along with its wheels was cut to pieces; / with one arrow he pierced his chest, and with one, the charioteer.
Filling his conch, he roared with the sound of the conch; / [the enemy] praised that feat: "Well done, O mighty hero!"
Seeing that valour, the exceedingly glorious one, filled with wrath, / mounted another chariot and went to fight the prince.
He said, "O hero, behold my wonderful prowess!" / Having spoken thus, he quickly released torrents of sharp-jointed arrows.

Arrows were seen everywhere, upon elephants and upon horses; / like the supreme Brahman, they pervaded all and were within range everywhere.

Having quickly enveloped that prince with ten million sharp arrows, / the valorous one roared.

gladdening his own troops and making the enemy / completely void in heart, deprived of life.

That prince, seeing himself surrounded / by crowds of sharp arrows, was enraged.
Endowed with boundless prowess, the great one seized weapons / and, brandishing his bow in his pillar-like arms,
the mighty one cut down all missiles and weapons, / releasing arrows that tore through enemies, his eyes copper-red with rage.
Shaking off that mass of weapons, the prince said to him: / "Endure one blow of mine, if you are a hero, sir!
If I do not bring you down from your chariot with this, / then hear my vow, O hero, made out of my pride:
May the sin of those intoxicated people, skilled in sophistry, who censure the Veda— / which plunges one into the ocean of hell—belong to me!"
Having spoken thus, he drew from his quiver an excellent arrow / fierce like death, enveloped in circles of flame, and fitted it to his bow.
that arrow, released by the best of princes and aimed at the chest, / went swiftly toward him, equal in splendor to the fire of cosmic dissolution.
Pratāpāgrya, seeing the arrow aimed to cause his downfall, / then placed sharp arrows on his bow to cut down that shaft.
Splitting all those arrows right through their middle, / that shaft indeed went straight into Pratāpāgrya's steadfast chest.
The iron arrow struck the chest and penetrated inside it; / and the king, struck down, fell to the surface of the earth.
Seeing him swooned, unconscious, fallen from the chariot's seat to the earth, / his charioteer took him and bore him away from the battlefield.
A great outcry arose, and the defeated army then fled / to where that Śatrughna was, surrounded by crores of heroes.
The prince, having won victory and defeated Pratāpāgrya, / waited there for that king Śatrughna.

5.24.m: Śeṣa said: / Śatrughna, overcome with rage, grinding his teeth against teeth, / shaking his hands, repeatedly licked his lower lip with his tongue.
Again and again he asked them: "By whom has my horse been taken? / By whom has Pratāpāgrya, the crest-jewel of all heroes, been defeated?"
Those servants then said: "O slayer of foes, [a hero] named Damana, / the son of Subāhu, has defeated Pratāpāgrya and carried off the horse."
Hearing that the horse had been led away by his enemy Damana, / he came swiftly to where the battlefield was.
There that Śatrughna saw elephants with split temples / immersed in blood as if mountains, arrogant with rut.
Wounded horses together with their riders / lay dead there, seen by the greatly enraged Śatrughna.
Beholding the broken men, chariots, and elephants, that slayer of foes / grew exceedingly angry, like the ocean of dissolution at cosmic dissolution.
Seeing before him the formidable Damana, who had taken the horse / and conquered Pratāpāgrya, holding his own army as mere straw,
the king then spoke to the warriors, his eyes turbulent with anger: / "Who here will conquer Damana, who wields all weapons and missiles?
He who, fearless, will conquer with a missile that prince, / the hero skilled in the work of battle—let him be ready!"
Hearing these words, Puṣkala, slayer of enemy heroes, / resolved to defeat Damana, spoke these words:
"O lord, where is this wretched Damana, and where is your boundless might? / By your majesty I shall conquer him; I am going, O wise one!
When I, your servant, am present for battle, by whom can the horse be taken? / This majesty of Raghunātha will accomplish everything.
O lord, hear my vow that will bring you joy: / I shall conquer in battle Damana, who is expert in the actions of war."
Whatever sin belongs to those deprived of tasting the honey of Rāmacandra's lotus feet, / may that sin be mine if I do not conquer Damana!"
Whatever darkness falls upon a son who, considering any sacred place other than his mother's feet, / quarrels with her, may that [sin] be mine if I do not conquer Damana!
Today let that prince, his broad chest pierced by my arrows, / adorn the surface of the earth by lying upon it in battle!"
Śeṣa said: / Hearing this vow of Puṣkala, the descendant of Raghu, / radiant, rejoiced in his heart and directed [him] toward battle.
Thus commanded, he went forth, surrounded by vast forces, / to where Prince Damana was, born of a line of heroes.
Recognizing that he had arrived at the battleground, Damana too, / foremost among heroes, went forth surrounded by his own army.
The two met each other, standing in chariots, shining in their chariots, / as if Śakra and the Daitya had come to the battlefield for combat.
Puṣkala spoke to that prince of great might: / "O Prince Damana, know that I have arrived!
Vowed to battle, the formidable son of Bharata, / known by the name of Puṣkala, know me [as such], O best of men!
A bee to the perpetual service of Raghunātha's lotus feet, / I shall conquer you with a multitude of weapons! Make ready, O high-minded one!"
Hearing these words, Damana, slayer of enemy heroes, / an eloquent speaker whose valour had been seen, laughed and fearlessly replied:
"Know me as Damana, the son of Subāhu, whose sins are dispelled by devotion to his father, / the captor of the horse of King Śatrughna!
Victory is granted by fate; whomever it will adorn, / that one attains it. Behold my might at the forefront of the battle!"
Having spoken thus, drawing his arrow-fitted bow all the way to his ear, / he released sharp arrows that take away the lives of enemies.
Those arrows, becoming dense, covered the sky; / where the brilliance of the sun's rays was blocked by the shadow of the arrows,
the continuous flight of shafts, striking the temples of the elephants, / adorned them like variegated mineral pigments.
Fallen there were seen men, horses, elephants, and chariots, / thoroughly struck down by the multitude of the prince's arrows.
Seeing that valor, Puṣkala, slayer of enemy heroes, / and seeing the battleground covered by the shadow of arrows,
placed on his bow an arrow consecrated by Agni; / sipping water according to rule, he released the shaft.
Then fire appeared there at the forefront of battle, / licking the sky with flames, as if the fire of cosmic dissolution had arisen.
Then his army, scorched, was seized with terror on the battlefield, / and took to flight, tormented by the flames of fire.
The moon-shaped parasols of the archers were burnt; / there they were seen possessing the luster of the color of gold.
Burnt horses of the enemies fled with their manes ablaze; / the chariots too were consumed by fire along with their fine poles.
Then young camels, carrying gems, rubies, and jewels, / fled, tormented by the mass of flames from the blazing earth.

In some places elephants perished, in other places horsemen;
in other places foot-soldiers perished, their bodies burned by fire.

All the arrows discharged by the prince met destruction;
they were turned to ashes on all sides by the flames of the fire.

Then, when his own army was burned, Damana, filled with rage,
knowing all weapons, took up the Vāruṇa weapon to quench it.

The Vāruṇa weapon, released by that king's son to quench the fire,
inundated the other's army, filled with chariots and horses.

The chariots of the adversaries were seen flooded in the water,
and his own elephants, though scorched, obtained relief.

And the fire subsided, discharged as it had been by the fire-weapon;
his own army, tormented by the flames of fire, attained relief.

Trembling from the cold water, the adversaries cried out in distress,
pelted by showers of hail and battered by the wind.

Then, seeing his own army afflicted by the flood of water,
trembling, agitated, lost, and carried away by the Vāruṇa weapon,

Puṣkala, the son of Bharata, his eyes copper-red with intense anger,
fixed upon his bow a single great arrow, the Vāyavya weapon.

Then a mighty wind arose, propelled by the Vāyavya weapon;
it swiftly destroyed the gathered army of clouds.

Elephants were hurled by the wind and dashed against one another;
and horses were thrown against each other along with their riders.

Men, tossed by the gale, with disheveled hair and drained of vigor,
were seen falling here like vetālas fallen to the earth.

Seeing his entire army overwhelmed by the wind,
that prince fixed the mountain-weapon upon his bow.

Then mountains fell upon the heads of the combatants;
covered by them, the wind no longer blew anywhere.

Puṣkala, however, fixed [the weapon] called Vajra upon his bow;
cut by the Vajra, all those [mountains] became sesame-seed sized in an instant.

The Vajra, having reduced the mountains to mere dust, consecrated as an arrow,
fell with great noise and force upon the prince's chest.

With his mind bewildered, pierced in the heart and severely wounded,
the mighty hero suffered; he fell into a deep swoon.

Seeing him fallen into a swoon, the charioteer, skilled in prudent conduct,
carried the prince away from that battle to a distance of just one krośa.

Then the warriors of the prince, scattered and fled,
went to the city and reported the king's son lying in a swoon.

Puṣkala, having thus gained victory at the front of battle, knowing dharma,
was unable to strike again, remembering the word of Raghunātha.

Then there was the sound of kettledrums and a great roar of victory,
and pleasing shouts arose: “Bravo! Bravo!”

Śatrughna experienced joy upon seeing Puṣkala victorious;
surrounded by ministers such as Sumati, he praised him.

5.25.m: Śeṣa said: / Then the king, seeing his own soldiers with their limbs bathed in a flood of blood, / found no comfort, grieved for them, and asked about the conduct of his son:
“Tell all of his deeds! How did he seize that excellent horse? / And tell, alas, how large an army, how many heroes came to fight?
Then facing the enemy army, how did my heroic Damana wage battle? / And having achieved victory, alas, did someone strike down that hero who is difficult to conquer?”
Hearing the king's words, his servants, / whose bodies and clothes were drenched in blood, replied:
“O King, having seen the horse adorned with the inscribed leaf and marks, / he seized it with pride, making light of the best of the Raghus.
Then the guardian of the horse arrived, surrounded by a small force; / with him there was a tumultuous, hair-raising battle.
Then, having rendered him unconscious with his arrows, / while your son stood [in victory], Śatrughna arrived, surrounded by his own forces.
Then a great battle took place, filled with weapons and missiles; / many times your mighty son obtained victory.
Just now, having released a weapon, by that nephew of Śatrughna, / O King, your heroic son was rendered unconscious in battle.”
Hearing these words, he was filled with rage and sorrow; / with his limbs motionless, he was like the ocean on the full moon day.
With his lower lip quivering with rage, he spoke to his commander of the army, / gnashing his teeth, licking his lip with his tongue, emaciated by grief:
“O Commander of the Army, immediately make ready my army! / I will fight with the excellent warriors of Rāma, the slayers of my son.
Today, with sharp arrows, I will strike down the one who brought sorrow to my son, / even if Maheśvara himself should be his protector.”
Having heard this command spoken by King Subāhu, / the commander of the army carried it out and made himself ready.
He announced to the king the fourfold army made ready, / resembling the forces of death, destroyer of millions of wicked foes.
Hearing the commander's report, Subāhu, slayer of enemy heroes, / marched out to the place where Śatrughna, the afflicter of his son, was,
with rut-maddened elephants, horses swift as thought, / and chariots stocked with all weapons and missiles, conquerors of the foe.
And the earth trembled then under the immense weight of that army; / a very great tumult arose as the army marched forth there.
Seeing the king march out in a chariot made of gold, / Śatrughna's army prepared, ready to strike all enemies.
Suketu, his brother, skilled in mace-fighting, / came swiftly in a chariot filled with all weapons and missiles.
And Citrāṅga, the king's son, expert in every type of warfare, / went quickly in his own chariot against the furious army of Śatrughna.
His younger brother named Vicitra, skilled in extraordinary battle, / went in a golden chariot, distressed by his brother's suffering.
Other heroic, mighty archers, skilled in all weapons and missiles, / commanded by the king, went to the battle filled with heroes.
King Subāhu, arriving in fury at the battlefield, / beheld his son unconscious, tormented by arrows.
Seeing his son named Damana lying senseless in the chariot-box, / he was overwhelmed with grief again and again, and fanned him with leafy twigs.
Sprinkled with water and touched by the king with his gentle hand, / the heroic Damana, knower of supreme weapons, slowly regained consciousness.
Rising, [he said:] “Where is my bow? Where has Puṣkala gone from here, / abandoning the battle after engaging, tormented by the wounds of my arrows?”
Hearing these words spoken by his son, Subāhu / felt supreme joy and embraced his son.
Damana, seeing his father the king, bowed his head / and fell at his feet with devotion, his body wounded by lines of missiles.
Having placed his son back in the chariot, the king, / skilled in the art of war, spoke again to his army commander:

“Form in the battle the Krauñca array, unconquerable by foes, / entering which I may conquer the army of King Śatrughna.”

Hearing those words of King Subāhu, / he drew up the excellent battle array known as the heron.
which the enemy host, though very mighty and bearing masses of weapons, / could not easily penetrate.
Suketu stood at its beak, Citrāṅga at its neck; / the two princes were at the two wings, and the king was stationed at the tail.
In its center was his great army, adorned with the four divisions. / Having formed the intricate heron-shaped battle formation, he reported it to the king.
The king, seeing the heron-shaped battle formation well prepared and skillfully constructed, / set his mind on battle with those who stood in Śatrughna’s camp.
